entities.name: Craterus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Craterus (b. 369 BCE, Macedonia) emerged as one of the most distinguished generals and trusted companions of Alexander the Great, playing a pivotal role in the Macedonian conquest of the Achaemenid Empire and the subsequent tumultuous Wars of the Diadochi. His career, spanning the height of Alexander's power and the immediate fragmentation of his empire, positioned him as a major contender for regency and control over the Hellenistic world. Recognised for his steadfast loyalty and military acumen, Craterus's influence was felt across the vast territories from Greece to India.

During Alexander's campaigns, Craterus commanded the hypaspists and later the entire phalanx, distinguishing himself in critical engagements such as the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BCE) and the Battle of Gaugamela (331 BCE). His pragmatic leadership was evident during the mutiny at the Hyphasis River, where he advocated for the army's return to Macedon. Alexander entrusted him with the crucial task of leading 10,000 veteran soldiers back to Europe in 324 BCE, along with the responsibility of installing Antipater as satrap of Cilicia, demonstrating the immense trust placed in him by the king.

Following Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Craterus became a central figure in the power struggles known as the Wars of the Diadochi. He allied with Antipater, solidifying their bond through marriage to Antipater’s daughter, Phila. This alliance aimed to secure control over Macedon and Greece against other ambitious generals. His unexpected death in battle against Eumenes of Cardia in 320 BCE, while fighting in Cappadocia, removed a significant military and political force, dramatically altering the balance of power among the Diadochi and contributing to the further fragmentation of Alexander’s envisioned empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Craterus was a major general who helped forge Alexander's empire and, through his death in 320 BCE, critically altered the early power dynamics of the Wars of the Diadochi, contributing to the ultimate division of Alexander's empire into successor kingdoms.
